newsitem.title: UK: Strong goes as fails to revitalise Sears.
newsitem.headline: Strong goes as fails to revitalise Sears.

text.p: Liam Strong, whose job as chief executive of British retailer Sears Plc was taken away after it announced break-up plans on Tuesday, will leave after failing to revitalise the Selfridges-to-shoes group following five years in charge.

Everyone agreed that Strong faced an uphill battle when he became chief executive in 1992, hired from the newly privatised British Airways to improve returns from the mixed bag of Sears retail businesses, including its troubled British Shoe Corporation.
There were hopes that Strong could stem the group's long-term decline and put new life into its tired retail formats.
But Strong's performance failed to please long-suffering Sears shareholders.
Retail industry analysts now say optimism was misplaced as Sears under Strong's control failed to deliver any sustained improvement in performance since the recession of the early 1990s.
Shareholders began to lose patience when Strong's actions did not produce the goods and he seemed increasingly accident-prone.
Last year Sears had to take back shoe stores which Strong had sold to retailer Facia when Facia collapsed.

This year Sears had to issue a profit warning after a poor Christmas. And Strong's plans to sell Sears' Freemans mail order to retail and football pools firm Littlewoods ran into trouble when the deal was referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
Strong switched to an alternative buyer for the Freemans business, N.Brown Group Plc, to sidestep the MMC but had to go back to Littlewoods and accept a lower price when N.Brown pulled out.

He first promised shareholders a 410 million pound ($666 million) payout from the proceeds of selling Freemans but this has dropped to 370 million as Sears is getting less than originally expected from the sale.
These misfortunes prompted a rising tide of criticism in the British press, claiming that investors wanted Strong out and that Sears should be broken up.
Strong, now 52, made his name at British Airways as a marketing high flier. He joined the Sears board in 1991 and became chief executive in February 1992.
A fan of military history, with American Civil War general Ulysses S. Grant as one of his heroes, Strong began a campaign to knock Sears into shape.
He sold off loss-making businesses such as Fosters, Olympus, Ter Meulen Post and Sears Andre and pruned British Shoe by reducing its 14 different retail brands to four.
But retail analysts said the surgery was not radical enough, prompting calls for a break-up to unlock value in the Selfridges department store operation and womenswear and get rid of British Shoe.
The break-up has finally happened and has effectively got rid of Strong's job.
Sears in its new guise will be run by Vittorio Radice, the boss of Selfridges, and Derek Lovelock, who is in charge of the clothing stores.
Chairman Sir Bob Reid will stay on and oversee both businesses.
Strong will walk away with a year's salary, worth around 400,000 pounds, plus pension and share benefits.

He began his career with U.S. consumer products group Procter and Gamble, moving to Reckitt and Colman in 1975. In 1989 he switched to British Airways, where he was director of marketing and operations.
Married with two children, his hobbies include walking, sailing, shooting and opera.
($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
